beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: For thousands of years, God had been speaking. Never all at once. Never the whole picture. But always, patiently, reaching toward people who could barely hear him.

beats.speaker: scripture
beats.text: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,

timing.text: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: In many times, and in many different ways. To one he spoke from a bush that burned but would not burn up. To another, in fire that fell on a mountain.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: To one he gave words to write on a scroll in the lamplight. Another he sent to cry out in the city gate to people who mostly would not listen. A fragment here, a flash there — true, but partial.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Century after century, messenger after messenger, each one carrying a piece of it. Never quite the whole. Never a face you could look full into and say, so that is what God is like.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: And then, after all the fragments, God did something he had never done. He stopped sending messages about himself — and came in person.

beats.text: Not another prophet with another piece. The Son. God's own last and clearest word, spoken not in fire on a mountain, but in a real human life you could walk beside.

beats.text: The exact likeness of God, in a face you could actually look at. If you have ever wondered what God is really like — whether he is angry, or distant, or cold — the answer is not a guess. Look at Jesus. That is God, saying everything, at last.

card.text: For ages God spoke in fragments; then he said it all in a Son. His clearest word about himself is a warm human face inviting you in. If you want to know what God is really like, where might you start looking?
